newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW-Rolls bullish on civil aeroengine market.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Rolls bullish on civil aeroengine market.

text.p: The chairman of Rolls-Royce Plc said on Thursday the aero-engine firm's productivity gains of the last few years would allow it to make money from an Airbus engine deal which saw strong bidding from U.S. rival Pratt & Whitney.

Ralph Robins told Reuters the supply deal for its Trent 500 engine for Airbus Industrie's A340 derivatives, the A340-500 and A340-600, would show a "good internal rate of return". He declined to give the figure.

Earlier at the Paris air show Karl Krapek, president of United Technologies Corp's Pratt & Whitney (P&W), said the company would have been out of pocket by $1.5 billion on the Airbus programme in the first eight years and needed 23 years to get a return on investment -- which would be below double digits.
Robins said his group's payback period "is very much lower than that. Our costs are much lower than theirs". P&W was bidding right up to the last minute at the air show, he said.
Rolls would keep development costs down by drawing on its family of engines, using components from the Trent 800 and Trent 700.
And with potential sales of 500 Airbus aircraft, each with four engines, Rolls would make money on the deal. "We like four-engine aircraft," Robins said.

The new Trent will deliver 56,000 pounds, with a potential upgrade to 68,000 pounds. It could be used for Boeing Co's 747 jumbo jet heavyweight derivative, the 747-400 IGW and the widebody 767-400, he said.
Rolls expects to deliver 40 percent more commercial engines this year compared with 1996. He said the present upswing in the industry would probably be durable.

"I think it's going to be a longer cycle. The airlines are more mature. The market is growing at 15 percent a year. In the last cycle it was over 30 percent," he said. "Airlines realise it's not in their interest to drive it too high".
Aircraft and engine manufacturers were hit hard when airlines flew into a deep recession in the early 1990s, just about the same time as defence spending was slashed after the fading of the Cold War.

"We are beginning to exploit this turn-up in the civil business and getting a payback on cost reductions and improvements in efficiency. We have been taking orders in almost every part of the range at the air show," Robins said.
The outlook for military sales, which account for 33 percent of group turnover, is "more stable".

The military side is turning out around 100 engines a year, after hitting a low point in 1994 when the Bristol plant in Britain produced 50. The present output would likely continue for the next few years, he said.

The acquisition of Allison in the United States had "helped dramatically" and gave Rolls a share in key programmes such as Lockheed Martin's Hercules C130J, the Bell-Boeing V22 Osprey tilt-rotor aircraft and the Comanche helicopter.
Technology which can be used for both military and commercial programmes will be increasingly important in the future, he said.
Military programmes consume little capital, governments fund research and development and they generate steady profit. "It's a good business," he added.
